title: The U.S. District Court for Hawaii Rules That a Medicare Advantage Plan Downstream Entity Can Sue for Double Damages
summary: The U.S. District Court for Hawaii has ruled that the assignee of a Medicare Advantage Plan (MAP) “downstream entity” can sue for double damages.
body_markdown:
\[1\] The court described downstream entities, generally, as “local entities \[that MAPs occasionally contract with\] that pay for a beneficiaries’ care.” *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *2.


Of note, the United States District Court for Maryland in its recent decision in *MAO-MSP Recovery II, LLC v. Government Employers Ins. Co.* , 2024 WL 2924063 (D. Maryland, June 10, 2024) provided a more detailed definition of a “downstream entity” (as well as a related entity known as a “first tier entity”) as follows:


As defined by CMS regulations, a ‘first tier entity’ is “any party that enters into a written arrangement, acceptable to CMS, with an \[MAO\] to provide administrative services or health care services for a Medicare eligible individual under the MA program,” and a “downstream entity” is ‘any party that enters into a written arrangement, acceptable to CMS, with persons or entities involved with the MA benefit, below the level of the arrangement between an \[MAO\] and a first tier entity.’ 42 C.F.R. § 422.2 Such entities can incur financial costs associated with making conditional payments or reimbursing MAOs for their conditional payments. *See MSP Recovery Claims, Series LLC v. ACE Am. Ins. Co.* , 974 F.3d 1305, 1314 (11th Cir. 2020). The GEICO Defendants assert that any conditional payments made by such entities are made pursuant to contracts with MAOs, not with CMS, so these entities have no statutory remedy to seek recovery for those payments. The GEICO Defendants cite no authority for this argument other than a district court case that was later abrogated by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. (citations omitted). *MAO-MSP Recovery II, LLC v. Government Employers Ins. Co.* , 2024 WL 2924063 (D. Maryland, June 10, 2024), at *9.


\[2\] The MSP’s private cause of action statute is codified at 42 U.S.C. 1395y(b)(3)(A) which states, in full, as follows: “There is established a private cause of action for damages (which shall be in an amount double the amount otherwise provided) in the case of a primary plan which fails to provide for primary payment (or appropriate reimbursement) in accordance with paragraphs (1) and (2)(A).” Id.


\[3\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *2. See also n. 1.


\[4\] The Ninth Circuit has jurisdiction over federal cases originating from Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, and Washington, along with the territories of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. See,[https://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/](https://www.ca9.uscourts.gov/)


\[5\] By way of note, the 3rd Circuit has jurisdiction over federal cases originating in Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands; the 11th Circuit has jurisdiction over federal cases originating in Alabama, Florida, and Georgia; while the Second Circuit has jurisdiction over federal cases originating in Connecticut, New York, and Vermont.


\[6\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *5.


\[7\] Id. at *2.


\[8\] Id.


\[9\] Id.


\[10\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *2, citing Dkt. No. 27, at PageID 767. On this point, the court stated in greater detail as follows: “The court dismissed Alpha Thirteen’s prior complaint—the First Amended Complaint, or ‘FAC’—for lack of jurisdiction. It reached that conclusion because the pleading “\[did\] not contain any facts tying C.G.’s alleged injury at the hand of OTS to MDX Hawaii’s ultimate assignment of its claims to Alpha Thirteen.” Dkt. No. 27, at PageID.767. In other words, what was missing was ‘any allegation that MDX Hawaii assigned the particular claims arising out of the injury caused by OTS to Alpha Thirteen.’ *Id.* While Alpha Thirteen pointed to a ‘Schedule 1’ as evidence that MDX Hawaii assigned its right to recover on claims paid out for C.G., that document did not provide a way “to discern which claims, if any, are related to injuries incurred as a result of C.G.’s bus accident, or indeed whether any Patient ID corresponds to C.G. at all.” *Id.* at PageID.768. Thus, as the court observed, “neither the First Amended Complaint nor Exhibit 1 alleges that any Patient ID listed on Schedule 1 is in fact C.G.” *Id.* On that ground, the court granted OTS’ motion to dismiss and did not address any of the other contentions OTS made in its motion to dismiss. *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *2.


\[11\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *2.


\[12\] ** Id. at *3.


\[13\] Id.


\[14\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *3. On these points, the court stated, in full, as follows: “Alpha Thirteen’s SAC has shown that MDX Hawaii would have had the right to sue on its own. First, the facts alleged in the SAC establish that MDX Hawaii suffered an injury-in-fact when it made payments on behalf of Medicare enrollee C.G. *See* Dkt. No. 28, at PageID.781–82; Dkt. No. 34, at PageID.1364–1483. Second, these injuries are fairly traceable to OTS. Unlike in the FAC, which the court previously determined lacked the “factual connective tissue” linking “C.G.’s alleged injury at the hands of OTS to MDX Hawaii’s ultimate assignment of its claims to Alpha Thirteen,” the SAC cures these defects. Dkt. No. 28, at PageID.783; Dkt. No. 25, at PageID.1486–88. In its SAC, Alpha Thirteen lists only entries related to the accident-related injuries that MDX Hawaii paid on behalf of C.G. Dkt. No. 28, at PageID.783; Dkt. No. 35, at PageID.1486-88. And third, the injury is redressable by a favorable decision through the requested compensation. Dkt. No. 28, at PageID.787. Thus, the court concludes that the facts alleged in the SAC adequately establish standing." Id.


\[15\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *4. Regarding the Hawaii MDX’s assignment to Alpha Thirteen as plead in the SAC, the court stated: “The SAC also sufficiently alleges that MDX Hawaii validly assigned its claim to Alpha Thirteen. The unredacted SAC identifies the alleged Assignor as ‘MDX Hawaii,’ the alleged Assignee as ‘Alpha Thirteen,’ and the date of the assignment. It also describes the essential terms of the assignment agreements, including that ‘Assignor hereby irrevocably and absolutely sells, assigns, grants, conveys, transfers, and sets over to Assignee ... all Legal Claims arising from or related to Assignor’s payment of the Identified Medical Claims.’ Dkt. No. 34, at PageID.1261. In light of these factual allegations in the SAC, the court concludes that Alpha Thirteen pleads sufficient facts giving rise to subject matter jurisdiction. *Accord* *MAO-MSO Recovery II, LLC v. Farmers Ins. Exch.* , No. 17-cv-02559, 2018 WL 2106467, at *8 (C.D. Cal. May 7, 2018) (holding that pleadings were sufficient where they identified the alleged assignors, assignees, date of the assignments, and essential terms of the agreement).” Id.


\[16\] *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *4.


\[17\] As part of its argument, OTS contended that a narrow reading of the PCA statute was applicable given that MAPs are afforded a recovery right under a separate statutory provision, 42 U.S.C. 1395w-22(a)(4) under the MAP statutes. As such, OTS argued that because Congress has created a separate method for MAPs to seek recovery, it must not have authorized MAPs to also sue under the MSP’s PCA statute.


The court, however, rejected this argument based on the Ninth Circuit’s ruling in *Parra v. Pacificare of Arizona, Inc.* 715 F.3d 1146 (9th Cir. 2013).


In this regard, the court stated: “One problem with OTS’s argument is that it clashes with Ninth Circuit precedent: to the extent a MAO-specific provision exists for recovering past payments, the Ninth Circuit has suggested that it does not lend itself to an independent cause of action. In *Parra v. PacifiCare of Arizona, Inc.* , the Ninth Circuit held that while § 1395w-22(a)(4) ‘allows recovery from a primary plan that refuses to reimburse the MAO for payments made on behalf of a participant,’ it does not create a private right of action. (citation omitted). Instead, it ‘simply allows \[a MAO\] to provide via its contracts that its insurance is secondary to other available plans” and to bring a contracts claim to recoup those costs. (citations omitted) Hence, permitting MAOs to assert a double-damages cause of action under § 1395y(b)(3)(A) would not, as OTS argues, ‘substantially diminish the independent work performed by Congress’ separate Medicare Advantage provision.’ (citation omitted). In fact, excluding MAOs from availing themselves of § 1395y(b)(3)(A) would run contrary to regulations, which provide that MAOs “exercise the same rights to recover from a primary plan, entity, or individual that the Secretary exercises under the \[Medicare Secondary Payer\] regulations in subparts B through D of part 411 of this chapter.” 42 C.F.R. § 422.108(f).” *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *6.


Expanding on the above point, the court further noted that Ninth Circuit “referenc\[ed\] this very regulation to support its holding that the MAO statute § 1395w-22(a)(4) does not itself create a federal cause of action for MAOs. (citation omitted). But the court referenced that line in interpreting whether the MAO statute created a private right of action, not in interpreting whether the MSP Act’s enforcement provision § 1395y(b)(3)(A) could be asserted by MAOs. (citation omitted). The distinction, while fine, is significant. The former goes to whether a statute should be interpreted as creating a private cause of action; the latter, which is already recognized as a cause of action, goes to whether that cause of action is open to certain actors. And insofar as the *Parra* court’s statements could be construed to foreclose MAOs from the double-damages private cause of action, any ambiguity is removed by its clarification that it was not resolving whether § 1395y(b)(3)(A) ‘provided a MAO a private right of action against third-party tortfeasors for medical expenses advanced on behalf of plan participants.’” (citation omitted) *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *6.


\[18\] See also, n. 4.


\[19\] On this point, the court stated: “This issue is one of first impression in the Ninth Circuit, but all other circuits to have interpreted the statute—the Second, Third, and Eleventh Circuits—have rejected the position OTS advances here. \[footnote omitted\]. In *In re Avandia Marketing, Sales Practices and Products Liability Litigation* , the Third Circuit determined that ‘\[t\]he language of the MSP private cause of action is broad and unrestricted and therefore allows any private plaintiff with standing to bring an action.’ 685 F.3d 353, 367 (3d. Cir. 2012). The Eleventh Circuit relied on a similar reasoning, concluding that it saw ‘no basis to exclude MAOs from a broadly worded provision that enables a plaintiff to vindicate harm caused by a primary plan’s failure to meet its MSP primary payment or reimbursement obligations.’ *Humana Med. Plan, Inc. v. Western Heritage Ins. Co.* , 832 F.3d 1229, 1238 (11th Cir. 2022). And the Second Circuit is in accord. *Aetna Life Ins. Co. v. Big Y Foods, Inc.* , 52 F.4th 66, 73 (2d Cir. 2022) (agreeing with and quoting from the Third and Eleventh Circuits’ decisions and observing that the provision ‘provides no limitation on which private actors may sue a primary plan that fails to provide reimbursement’).” *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *5; see also, n. 17.


In addition to the above, the court noted that “\[a\]lthough the Ninth Circuit has not yet opined on whether the MSP Act allows MAOs and downstream entities to rely on the double-damages provision, it has interpreted the meaning of the provision in other contexts. In *DaVita, Inc. v. Virginia Mason Memorial Hospital* , the Ninth Circuit ruled on the question of whether § 1395y(b)(3)(A) ‘require\[d\] payment by Medicare as a prerequisite to suit.’ 981 F.3d 679, 692 (9th Cir. 2020). It held that it did not. But the Ninth Circuit left unanswered the question currently before this court, its holding is in no way inconsistent with the decisions of the Second, Third, and Eleventh Circuits that the statute extends the double-damages private cause of action remedy to MAOs. *Alpha Thirteen v. OAHU Transit Services, Inc* . 2026 WL 3269908 (D. Hawaii, October 30, 2026), at *7, n. 3.

Government Employers Ins. Co.* , 2024 WL 2924063 (D. Maryland 2024); **Massachusetts** : *MSP Recovery Claims Series LLC v. Plymouth Rock Assurance Corporation* , 404 F.Supp.3d 470 (D. Co. v. Bi-Lo, LLC* , 2019 WL 4643582 (D. South Carolina 2019); **Tennessee** : *Cariten Health Plan, Inc. v. Mid-Century Ins. Co.,* No.: 2015 WL 5449221(E.D. Tenn. 2015); **Texas** : *Humana Ins. Co. v. Farmers Tex. Cnty. Mut. Ins. Co* ., 95 F.Supp.3d 983 (W.D. Tex. 2014 *) and* *Humana v. Shrader,* 584 B.R. 658 (S.D. Tex. 2018) *; and **Virginia** :* *Humana Ins. Co. v. Paris Blank LLP,* 187 F. Supp.3d 676 (E.D. Va. 2016).
